title: Fill a bucket to the brim from a garden hose's trigger nozzle, then stop the water
instruction: Pick up the hose nozzle, fill the blue bucket to the brim with it, then stop the water. Don't let it overflow or spill.
context: Filling a bucket from a hose is an everyday yard chore (washing a car, mixing, watering, animal water). It takes a tool picked up off the ground with a hose dragging on it, aimed with one hand and run with the other through a sprung trigger, and a stop timed by watching the water rise: too early leaves it short, too late runs it over.
setup: Two YAM arms at the station table. The table top is laid with a patio of 200 x 200 x 12 mm grey concrete pavers in running bond (ground surface 12 mm above the table, x 0.10-0.90 m, y -0.60-0.60 m; arm bases at x 0, y +-0.305). A blue polypropylene pail (0.38 kg empty; inside 180 mm across at the floor and 220 mm at the brim, 200 mm deep, brimful 6.30 L; rolled rim, one stiffening rib, steel wire bail lying down on its -x side) stands empty and free on the pavers, centred at (0.46, -0.04). A brick pillar 115 x 115 x 160 mm with a brass hose tap (outlet 95 mm above the ground, pointing down, handwheel red) stands at (0.66, 0.50); the tap is open throughout. A 1.24 m green 5/8 inch garden hose (22 mm outside, 0.35 kg/m full of water) runs from the tap's outlet in a loop over the pavers (left of the pail) to the nozzle. The nozzle is a pistol-grip spray nozzle (0.24 kg; satin zinc barrel, green rubber grip on the barrel 44 mm long with flats 28 mm apart, green rubber handle 100 mm long hanging behind the barrel, brass hose swivel at the handle's foot, 52 mm pattern dial set to flood, outlet 10 mm) with a 25 g chrome trigger hinged under the barrel in front of the handle. The trigger's return spring holds it against its rest with 0.26 N m and takes 0.75 N m at its 22 deg stop; water starts at 6 deg of squeeze and is fully on (12 L/min) from 20 deg. The nozzle lies on its left side on the pavers, its barrel's grip centred at (0.300, 0.150), the barrel pointing back and to the left (turned 120 deg from straight ahead), the handle toward the robot's right. Code (parts.py) gives every dimension and pose.
scoring: Water is measured as litres in the pail, litres that missed it, and litres that ran over the brim (missed + run over = spilled). Full: the water's surface within 15 mm of the brim (at least 5.73 L of 6.30 L). Score 0 if the pail tips more than 15 deg at any moment, or if more than 1.0 L is spilled. Otherwise 1.0 if the pail is full, the water has been off (trigger released past 6 deg) for at least 1 s, and at most 0.25 L has been spilled; else 0.75 with at least 85% of the brimful volume in the pail (5.36 L), 0.5 with at least 50% (3.15 L), 0.25 with at least 25% (1.58 L), and 0 below that. A real trial measures the level with a ruler from the rim, the pail's water by weighing it, and spills by a tarp under the pavers or a wet-area photo.
run_limit: 1,600 control steps at 20 Hz (80 s). The scripted demo reaches full score at 47.4 s.
reset_notes: Empty and dry the pail; dry the pavers; lay the hose back in its loop and the nozzle on its side at the start pose (see setup.png); the trigger is sprung and returns by itself. Use object_jitter=0 for the fixed layout. Real trials: cover the robot's bases and electronics against splashes and stand the patio on a tarp or drip tray, which also catches spills for weighing.
fidelity: The hose is 31 rigid 40 mm links joined by sprung, damped joints (bending stiffness about 0.02 N m^2), so it drags, hangs and pulls on the nozzle; the nozzle, trigger (a sprung hinge with a hard stop) and pail are rigid bodies held by contact only. The water is not a fluid simulation: each control step the valve's flow follows the trigger's measured angle, the stream is traced ballistically from the outlet (exit speed from flow and the 10 mm outlet) and counted into the pail if it reaches the water, floor or inner wall, or as spilled if it strikes the outer wall, the rim's top or the ground; water above the brim runs over and is spilled. The pail's mass grows with the water in it (1 kg per litre). The water, stream, foam and wet patches are drawn from that model. Splashing, the stream breaking up or hitting the robot, sloshing and water in the hose are not modelled.
